report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

table.title: Herding dog survey
table.data_collection_started: No, no data have been collected for this study yet.
table.research_questions:
Research Question 1 (RQ1): Which personality and behavioral traits in dogs are associated with owner-reported overall herding ability?
Research Question 2 (RQ2):  Do personality and behavioral traits in dogs and owner-rated overall herding ability predict herding performance in competitions?
Research Question 3 (RQ3): Do personality and behavioral traits in dogs and owner-rated herding ability differ across breeds and countries?
table.design_dependent_variables:
Dog personality traits will be measured via owner report in an online survey. The instruments included in the survey are based on the Livestock Working (Herding) Dog Assessment Form (LWHDAF) designed by McGreevy et al. (2015). The LWHDAF was designed to measure herding dog personality traits and behavioral traits. Recently, Wilson et al. (2022) used a revised version of the personality portion of the LWHDAF to construct the Herding Dog Assessment Form-Personality (HDAF-P). The present study will use both the HDAF-P and the behavioral portion of the original LWHDAF. The HDAF-P will be directly replicated, and the behavioral items on the LWHDAF will be modified. Modifications to the LWHDAF are intended to 1) make items more comparable to the HDAF-P and 2) increase participant understanding of the herding terminology used in the instrument.

Owner ratings of overall herding ability will be obtained using a single item in the online survey. The item asks the owner to rate their dog's "overall herding ability" on a five-point scale from "one of the worst dogs I have ever seen/trained" to "one of the best dogs I have ever seen/trained."

Herding performance will be measured using competition scores from two national herding dog competitions in the United States. Each competing dog will receive scores from a group of judges after performing a set of herding tasks on an obstacle course.
table.study_design_overview: This study is not experimental and will not involve assigning participants to conditions
table.statistical_tests:
RQ1: Research Question 1 will be evaluated by first (A) replicating the analyses used by Wilson et al. (2022) and then (B) expanding the analyses to include dog behavioral traits as a predictor.

A: Wilson and colleagues investigated the association between dog personality traits and owner ratings of overall herding ability. Correlation tables will be used to determine which personality scale items are strongly correlated with each other. A principal components analysis (PCA) will identify which personality traits are clustered together and how each component impacts the variance in the sample. We will conduct a mixed methods regression of the components to determine which components best predict owner-rated overall herding ability. Fixed effects will include the identified components as well as dog sex, gonad removal, age, and work environment. Following Wilson et al., we will first perform a series of univariate fixed effects regressions with owner included as a random effect. A reverse stepwise method based on Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) will be used for model selection. We will report both frequentist and Bayesian statistics. However, interpretations for the first part of RQ1 will draw on the frequentist statistics (i.e. p values) for ease of comparison with Wilson et al. (2022).

B: The second set of analyses for RQ1 will include both personality traits and behavioral traits as predictors for owner-rated overall herding ability. Correlation tables and a PCA will again be used to identify principal components. We will conduct a mixed methods regression with the components of the PCA as predictors of overall herding ability. Components that fall above the inflection point on the scree plot will be considered as predictors for the regression model. Any other fixed effects (e.g., dog sex) that are included in the final selected model for part A will be automatically included in the models for part B. Dog and owner will be considered as random effects. Model selection will be based on Bayes Factors calculated from Bayes Information Criteria (BIC). A Bayes factor of at least 3 must be achieved for the reference model to be rejected in favor of the more complex model. If more than one model exceeds a Bayes factor of 3, then the model with the greatest Bayes factor will be chosen. Starting with the intercept-only model as the reference model, we will use Bayes factors to determine whether including random effects in the model increases the fit of the model. If no random effects model has a Bayes factor of at least 3 when tested against the intercept-only, then the intercept-only model will be selected as the reference model for fixed effect model selection. Each fixed effects model will start from the reference model and include the fixed effects from part A. Assuming that random effects will be included in the new reference model, each fixed effects model will start with the same function stem (overall_ability ~ random_effects + fixed_effects_fromPartA). Every possible combination of PCA components will be added on the end of the function stem. For example, one fixed effects model will be (overall_ability ~ random_effects + fixed_effects_fromPartA + comp1) and another will be (overall_ability ~ random_effects + fixed_effects_fromPartA + comp1 + comp2). The fixed effects models will each be compared against the reference model (with no fixed effects). The Bayes factor criteria outlined above will be used to select the final best model. Inferences will be drawn from Bayes factors.

RQ2 will be evaluated using a principal components analysis and mixed methods regression. If the subset of the total study sample that has both survey and competition score data is large enough to be appropriate for principal components analysis, we will run a PCA on the personality and behavioral traits. Appropriate sample size for a PCA is relative to communality of the factors. MacCallum et al. (1999) suggest that a sample size of less than 100 observations is sufficient for the use of PCA if the average communality for all variables is 0.6 or greater. Therefore, we will use an average communality of 0.6 as the cutoff for an appropriately large sample. If the average communality is below 0.6, the components identified in RQ1 part B will be used for RQ2 analyses.
We will run a mixed methods regression with competition score as the outcome variable and the identified components and overall herding ability rating as predictors of interest. Dog sex, gonad removal, age, and work environment will be considered as other fixed effects. Dog and owner will be considered as random effects. Model selection will be based on Bayes factors calculated from Bayes Information Criteria (BIC). A Bayes factor of at least 3 must be achieved for the reference model to be rejected in favor of the more complex model. If more than one model exceeds a Bayes factor of 3, then the model with the greatest Bayes factor will be chosen. Starting with the intercept-only model as the reference model, we will use Bayes factors to determine whether including random effects in the model increases the fit of the model. If no random effects model has a Bayes factor of at least 3 when tested against the intercept-only, then the intercept-only model will be selected as the reference model for the next round of model selection.
The next round of model selection will focus on the fixed effects that are not the variables of interest in the study (e.g., sex, age). Each fixed effect will individually be tested against the reference model. If any fixed effect models have a Bayes factor of 3 or more, then further model testing will occur. All possible combinations of relevant fixed effects (as identified by Bayes factors ≥ 3) will be tested against the reference model. The best model at this stage will be selected based on the Bayes factor criteria. If no individual fixed effects models have a Bayes factor of at least 3 then the reference model will kept for the next round of selection.
Each model in the next round of selection will build on the reference model. Assuming that both random effects and fixed effect will be included in the reference model, each new model will start with the same function stem (competition_score ~ random_effects + fixed_effects). Every possible combination of the predictors of interest (PCA components and overall ability rating) will be added on the end of the function stem. For example, one model will be (competition_score ~ random_effects + fixed_effects + overall_ability) and another will be (competition_score ~ random_effects + fixed_effects + overall_ability + comp1). The new models will each be compared against the reference model. The Bayes factor criteria outlined above will be used to select the final best model. Inferences will be drawn from Bayes factors.

RQ3 will be evaluated by comparing data from the present study to Wilson et al.'s findings. Wilson and colleagues used a sample of Australian kelpies (a breed of dog). The present study sample will be American dogs and we expect that the majority of the sample will be border collies (a breed of dog). For each personality trait, we will run a T-test to compare the two study samples. Owner-rated overall herding ability will also be compared across samples using a T-test. Both frequentist and Bayesian statistics will be reported. For RQ3, we will draw on the Bayesian statistics for interpretation.
table.outliers_and_exclusions: Individual survey items where participants answer "I don't know" will be excluded from analyses. Missing data (no response) will be excluded at the item level. No outliers will be defined for this study.
table.sample_size: Sample size will be determined by time constraints. We will use all available avenues to recruit as many participants as possible for the duration of the data collection period. Data collection will end on December 31 2024.
table.additional_comments:
We will conduct exploratory analyses to examine the effects of dog and owner experience with herding on outcome variables (owner rating of dog herding ability and competition score).

The personality and behavioral trait instruments used in this study are based on the instruments designed and used by McGreevy et al. (2015). If granted access to the data from that study, exploratory analyses may be used to compare across study samples. We will pool the data across the two study samples and repeat the PCA and regression analyses. A new variable, Sample (present study vs. McGreevy et al. (2015)), will be included in the models.

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 162 columns across 3 data files.
#### Issues Identified

3 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(File = c("gatesy-davis_stevens_2025.csv", "gatesy-davis_stevens_2025a.csv", "gatesy-davis_stevens_2025b.csv"), Column = c("dog_birth_date", "dog_birth_date", "DOB"), Issues = c("🔒 Personally Identifying Information — Column name suggests personal information (matched: birthdate)", "🔒 Personally Identifying Information — Column name suggests personal information (matched: birthdate)", "🔒 Personally Identifying Information — Column name suggests personal information (matched: dob)" )), row.names = c(NA, -3L), class = "data.frame") # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 20, FALSE) ```
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 3 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

text.text: The value of herding dogs depends on how effectively they perform their job.
Improving the rate of success for herding dogs requires understanding which dogs succeed and why.
The present study determines whether dog personality and behavioral traits can be used to predict herding performance.
We began by replicating Wilson and colleagues (2022), who found that personality traits predict herding ability in Australian kelpies.
We asked American owners of herding dogs to complete an online survey about their dog's (n = 335) personality, behavior, and herding ability.
We grouped related personality variables together in a principal components analysis to create dog personality traits.
Next, we determined whether any dog personality traits predicted herding ability.
We partially replicate Wilson et al.'s (2022) findings, with similar personality traits predicting herding ability.
We then expanded on the previous study by creating a new set of traits that also included behavioral variables.
The personality and behavior model captured the observed data better than the personality-only model.
Lastly, we compared the personalities in our American herding dog sample to Wilson et al's (2022) Australian kelpies.
text.formatted: Lastly, we compared the personalities in our American herding dog sample to <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Wilson et al's (2022)</ref> Australian kelpies.

text.text: The two groups of herding dogs were different on some key personality variables.
We propose that herding dog handlers and breeders should focus on key personality and behavioral traits when making decisions about herding dog career paths and training efforts.
Dogs often take on many roles in our lives; they can be companions and teammates and even family members (Bouma et al., 2023; McConnell et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Dogs often take on many roles in our lives; they can be companions and teammates and even family members <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Bouma et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">McConnell et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: They also can serve important working roles.
Herding dogs help with gathering and moving livestock such as cows and sheep.
In general, dogs excel at this job because it taps into desire to chase prey animals (Coppinger & Coppinger, 2001).
text.formatted: In general, dogs excel at this job because it taps into desire to chase prey animals <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Coppinger & Coppinger, 2001)</ref>.

text.text: Farmers have taken advantage of that prey drive to train dogs when, where, and how to chase.
Dogs that become effective herders are well worth the time and monetary investment, with the value of a herding dog's labor estimated at USD $34,396 (Arnott et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Dogs that become effective herders are well worth the time and monetary investment, with the value of a herding dog's labor estimated at USD $34,396 <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Arnott et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Over time, we have created specific herding breeds (e.g., border collie, kelpie) with the help of artificial selection.
However, dogs do not need to be a herding breed to herd livestock, and herding breeds do not always work on farms.
Many herding breeds are kept as pets with no "job" other than to keep their human company.
These companion-only dogs may encounter their farm counterparts at herding competitions, called trials, which are a recreational activity that turns herding into a sport.
Whether in a recreational or agricultural setting, owners want their dog to be able to effectively herd livestock.
Unfortunately, roughly one in five working farm dogs do not go on to become successful at their job (Arnott et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Unfortunately, roughly one in five working farm dogs do not go on to become successful at their job <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Arnott et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Farmers who rely on these dogs must decide when to continue investing resources and training in herding dogs for agricultural work.
The present study aims to inform herding dog owners about which traits they should focus on for career decisions and training to provide the best chances of success.
Herding dog success is, to some degree, in the eyes of the beholder.
An owner's perception of their dog's overall herding ability is a mental representation that is built up over time.
Each time the dog herds, the owner receives new information to incorporate into their mental representation.
That information could tell the owner something about their dog's personality.
We view personality as a "suite of correlated behaviors expressed either within a given behavioral context or across different contexts" (Sih et al., 2004).
text.formatted: We view personality as a "suite of correlated behaviors expressed either within a given behavioral context or across different contexts" <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Sih et al., 2004)</ref>.

text.text: While the term temperament overlaps with personality in the literature, we use personality here to maintain consistency with similar studies of herding dogs (Gartner, 2015; Jones & Gosling, 2005).
text.formatted: While the term temperament overlaps with personality in the literature, we use personality here to maintain consistency with similar studies of herding dogs <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Gartner, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Jones & Gosling, 2005)</ref>.

text.text: Within the herding context, dogs display herding behaviors; the maneuvers and abilities that are specifically useful for herding livestock.
The dog's personality and behavior then, in turn, influence their owner's mental representation of the dog's herding ability.
In this study, we focus on the relationship between owner's perceptions of their dogs' personality, behavior, and herding ability.
In the world of working dogs, personality traits may be the key to success.
Bolder dogs achieve greater success in working dog trials (Svartberg, 2002) and less fearful dogs successfully complete service dog training (Dollion et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Bolder dogs achieve greater success in working dog trials <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Svartberg, 2002)</ref> and less fearful dogs successfully complete service dog training <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Dollion et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: The impact of personality on working dog outcomes suggests that personality is a predictor worth exploring in herding dogs.
Dog owners' perceptions also point to personality traits as a key to herding success.
When asked to indicate which personality traits are valuable in herding dogs, owners tend to agree that motivation, confidence, friendliness, and trainability are desirable (Early et al., 2019).
text.formatted: When asked to indicate which personality traits are valuable in herding dogs, owners tend to agree that motivation, confidence, friendliness, and trainability are desirable <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Early et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: While each herding environment requires a slightly different skill set, herding dogs all share a similar set of core personality traits (Early et al., 2018).
text.formatted: While each herding environment requires a slightly different skill set, herding dogs all share a similar set of core personality traits <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Early et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Across contexts, dog owners believe that dog personality traits influence herding ability.
Owners' ratings of their own dog's herding ability support their belief in the power of personality.
Studies focused on a single herding breed, the kelpie, suggest that dog personality explains differences in both owner perceptions and dog behavior (McGreevy et al., 2015; Wilson et al., 2022).

text.text: Personality traits in kelpies predict owner ratings of herding ability (Wilson et al., 2022).

text.text: Owner perceptions of kelpie personalities also align with observed difference in how the dogs perform on behavioral tests (McGreevy et al., 2015).

text.text: This validation suggests that owner reports of dog personality not only relate to owners' perceptions of herding ability but may reflect actual behavioral differences displayed by herding dogs.
Herding dogs perform specific herding behaviors when moving livestock (Coppinger & Coppinger, 2001; Early et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Herding dogs perform specific herding behaviors when moving livestock <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Coppinger & Coppinger, 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Early et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: These behaviors enable the dogs to manipulate the direction of movement, pace, and dispersion of a group of livestock.
Dog owners consider these herding behaviors to be an important factor in a dog's herding ability (Early et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Dog owners consider these herding behaviors to be an important factor in a dog's herding ability <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Early et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: If one animal starts to separate from the group, the dog needs to recognize this and quickly bring them back to the group.
A dog's ability to anticipate this issue and act to rectify it is correlated with their overall herding ability (McGreevy et al., 2015).
text.formatted: A dog's ability to anticipate this issue and act to rectify it is correlated with their overall herding ability <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(McGreevy et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Behavioral measures are a common way to capture overall herding ability.
Herding competitions use scores that are based on the dog's herding behaviors and speed.
Success at herding competitions has been used to make breeding and purchasing decisions (Conessa & Mailhac, 2013).
text.formatted: Success at herding competitions has been used to make breeding and purchasing decisions <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Conessa & Mailhac, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: However, performance in competitions does not appear to be heritable (Storteig Horn et al., 2017).

text.text: Taking a different approach, the Swedish Sheepdog Society used trainer ratings of young dogs' personality and behavioral variables to assess herding.
Some of the traits measured by the Swedish Herding Trait Characterization are heritable (Arvelius & Klemetsdal, 2013).

text.text: Owner ratings of their dogs' behaviors may be linked to perceptions of their dogs' overall herding dog abilities.
Personality and herding behavior are both separately linked to overall herding ability.
In this study, we examine how personality and behavior variables can be combined to predict overall herding ability.

First, we investigate which dog personality traits best predict overall herding ability (Research Question 1) by replicating the methods of Wilson et al. (2022) in a population of American herding dogs.
text.formatted: First, we investigate which dog personality traits best predict overall herding ability (Research Question 1) by replicating the methods of <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Wilson et al. (2022)</ref> in a population of American herding dogs.

text.text: Then, we explore which combinations of dog personality and behavioral traits best predict overall herding ability (Research Question 2).
Lastly, we investigate whether dog personality and owner-rated herding ability differ across breeds and countries (Research Question 3).

All procedures were conducted in an ethical and responsible manner, in full compliance with all relevant codes of experimentation and legislation and were approved by the University of Nebraska-Lincoln Internal Review Board (project ID UNL-00023563).
All participants (dog owners) offered consent to participate, and they acknowledged that de-identified data could be published publicly.
Owners of herding dogs (n = 186) submitted online survey responses for a total of 390 individual dogs.
After removing responses that were missing data for all of our study variables (personality, behavior, ability rating), we had 373 usable observations.
Dog owners met eligibility criteria if they currently owned at least one working herding dog.
We defined working herding dog as any dog that has experience herding livestock.
Respondents had to be at least 19 years old, live in the United States, and understand English.
We recruited dog owners through a combination of recruitment methods.
We posted recruitment materials in Facebook groups dedicated to dog-or farm-related topics and asked individual owners to share recruitment materials with others.
We invited owners signed up for the Canine Cognition and Human Interaction Lab registry to participate in the study.
For a more targeted recruitment approach, we also attended the 2024 United States National Cattledog Finals in Iowa and invited owners at the event to participate in the study.

Lastly, we sent email study invitations to owners who competed in either the 2024 United States National Cattledog Finals or the 2024 United States National Sheepdog Finals and had an email address publicly available online.
The pre-registered (https://osf.io/mshq9) sample size was determined by time constraints.

text.text: Data collection began on September 15, 2024 and terminated on December 31, 2024.
The sample of herding dogs had 188 females (50.4%), 158 males (42.4%), and 27 dogs with no reported sex (7.2%).
Dog ages ranged from 0.4 to 18.6 years with a mean of 5.7 years.
On average, each participating owner had 3.26 dogs.

The sample (n = 373) consisted of purebred border collies (n = 239), Australian shepherds (n = 20), Australian cattle dogs (n = 14), other breeds recognized or unrecognized by the American Kennel Club (n = 89), and mixed breeds (n = 6).

The majority of the dogs (n = 231) had some experience with working in both farm and competition settings, while others had farm experience but no competition experience (n = 102) or experience working only in competition settings (n = 12).
Most dogs with farm experience work in a utility environment (both large and small spaces) (n = 248).

Some dogs also worked in yard environments (small spaces) (n = 111), paddock environments (large spaces) (n = 99), droving environments (travel over long distances) (n = 50), and truck environments (trucks transporting livestock) (n = 19).
Owners most commonly reported that dogs had one to three years of experience working on a farm.
Dogs with trial experience had competed in an average of 16.0 trials and most commonly had one to three years of experience.
We built and distributed online surveys through REDCap hosted at University of Nebraska-Lincoln (Harris et al., 2019 (Harris et al., , 2009)).

Herding Dog Assessment Form-Personality.
The present study directly reproduced the Herding Dog Assessment Form-Personality (HDAF-P) (Wilson et al., 2022) to capture personality traits of particular interest in herding dogs.

text.text: This instrument combines and modifies items from the Monash Canine Personality Questionnaire-Revised (Ley et al., 2009), the Herding Trait Characterization (Arvelius et al., 2013), and the Dog Impulsivity Assessment Scale (Wright et al., 2012).

text.text: The Herding Dog Assessment Form-Personality asks the respondent to indicate how well a specific personality variable (e.g. confidence) describes their dog.
Each item is on a 5-point Likert-type scale (1 = very low,2 = low,3 = average,4 = high,5 = very high), plus a sixth option of "I don't know."
The instrument includes 17 personality items.
We transformed all personality variables into centered z-scores for the analyses.

We used an adapted version of the Livestock Working (Herding) Dog Assessment Form (LWHDAF) (McGreevy et al., 2015), a large-scale survey of working dogs on farms in Australia developed as part of the University of Sydney Farm Dog Project.

text.text: The instrument includes one section on personality variables, one section on working maneuvers (behaviors) and herding variables, and one section on training.
The section on working maneuvers and herding variables was selected for adaptation and use in the present study.
We will refer to the herding maneuvers and variables as "behavioral variables" for the rest of the article.
For each item, we included a brief narrative description of the behavioral variable drawn from the definitions provided by McGreevy et al. (2015).

This differs from the personality variables measured by the HDAF-P. We transformed all behavioral variables into centered z-scores for the analyses.
Overall herding ability was measured using a single survey item.
The item read "overall herding ability" and asked the owner to rate their dog on a five-point scale.

text.text: Our first research question asks which personality in dogs are associated with owner-reported overall herding ability.

We evaluated the association between personality variables and overall herding ability by replicating Wilson et al.'s (2022) correlations between dog personality variables and owner ratings of overall herding ability.
text.formatted: We evaluated the association between personality variables and overall herding ability by replicating <ref type="bibr">Wilson et al.'s (2022)</ref> correlations between dog personality variables and owner ratings of overall herding ability.

text.text: In a separate analysis, we used a principal components analysis (PCA) with all of the personality variable to identify which personality variables clustered together and how each component impacted the variance in the sample.
Components that fell above the inflection point on a scree plot were selected for use.
We additionally ran a parallel analysis (Horn, 1965) to support the selection of components as predictors.
text.formatted: We additionally ran a parallel analysis <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Horn, 1965)</ref> to support the selection of components as predictors.

text.text: We applied the weightings from each component to dog's scores on each personality item to create new weighted scores.
We then summed the weighted scores across the personality items for each dog, producing a single weighted score for each dog.
We repeated the process for each selected component so that each dog had one score per component.
We then used the weighted scores for each component as variables in our regression analyses.
All of the components selected based on the scree plot were entered into the model for the selection process.

We used model selection to determine which combination of PCA components and fixed effects variables would be included in the best-fit linear mixed regression for predicting owner-rated overall herding ability.
Fixed effects included the identified components as well as dog sex, gonad removal, age, and work environment.
Following Wilson et al., we first performed a series of univariate fixed effects regressions with owner included as a random effect.

Each potential predictor variable (including the components) was run in its own linear regression with overall ability as the outcome variable (e.g., overall_ability ~dog_age + (1|owner_id) or overall_ability ~comp1 + (1|owner_id)).
A reverse stepwise method based on Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) was used for model selection.
We report Bayes factors for the correlations and regression model; however, we follow Wilson et al.'s (2022) approach by drawing on p-values and AIC for interpretations of the data.
text.formatted: We report Bayes factors for the correlations and regression model; however, we follow <ref type="bibr">Wilson et al.'s (2022)</ref> approach by drawing on p-values and AIC for interpretations of the data.

text.text: Our second research question asks which combination of personality and behavioral variables in dogs are associated with owner-reported overall herding ability.
We performed a second set of analyses that incorporated behavioral variables (in addition to personality variables) as predictors of overall herding ability.
We used a principal components analysis of both the personality and behavioral variables to identify principal components for the new model.
We conducted a linear mixed regression with the components of the principal components analysis as predictors of overall herding ability.
We selected components to include in the model as predictors based on a scree plot and supported by a parallel analysis.
We created weighted scores from each component to use as predictors in the model.
Any other fixed effects (e.g., dog sex) that were included in the final selected model for the replication were automatically included in the new models.
Dog (individual) and owner were considered as random effects and tested for inclusion in the best-fit model.
We based the previous model selection on AIC to replicate Wilson et al.'s (2022) selection methods.
text.formatted: We based the previous model selection on AIC to replicate <ref type="bibr">Wilson et al.'s (2022)</ref> selection methods.

text.text: For the model including both personality and behavioral variables as predictors, we chose to perform model selection based on Bayes factors calculated from Bayes Information Criteria (BIC).
Bayes factors provide the amount of evidence for the alternative model relative to a reference model (Wagenmakers et al., 2010; Wagenmakers, 2007).
text.formatted: Bayes factors provide the amount of evidence for the alternative model relative to a reference model <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Wagenmakers et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Wagenmakers, 2007)</ref>.

text.text: First, we used an intercept-only model as the reference model for the random effects models.
Models containing dog, owner, and dog nested in owner, were compared against the reference model.
A Bayes factor of at least 3 was required for the reference model to be rejected in favor of the alternative model.
If more than one model exceeds a Bayes factor of 3, then the model with the greatest Bayes factor was chosen.
If no random effects model had a Bayes factor of at least 3 when tested against the intercept-only, then the intercept-only model was selected as the reference model for fixed effect model selection.

To assess the fixed effects, we assigned a new reference model that included the random effect determined above and all fixed effects from the final personality-only model (overall_ability ~fixed_effects_fromPersonality + random_effects).
The alternative models included the reference model plus every possible combination of the selected PCA components.

For example, one fixed effects model was (overall_ability ~fixed_effects_fromPersonality + comp1 + random_effects) and another was (overall_ability ~fixed_effects_fromPersonality + comp1 + comp2 + random_effects).
These fixed effects models were each compared against the reference model including only the chosen random effects (or intercept-only model) and the fixed effects from the personality-only model.
We again used the Bayes factor criteria outlined above to select the final best fit model and based our interpretations on the Bayes factor of the model.
Our third research question asks whether dog personality and owner-rated herding ability differ across breeds and countries.
We addressed this question by comparing our American sample to Wilson et al.'s (2022) sample of Australian kelpies.

text.text: We ran a series of t-tests to compare each personality variable of the dogs in our sample to the dogs in Wilson et al.'s sample.
Similarly, we compared owner-rated overall herding ability across samples using a t-test.
Both frequentest and Bayesian statistics are reported, but we draw on the Bayes factors for interpretation.
Following Wilson et al.'s data analysis plan, both missing data and "I don't know" responses were treated as missing data.
Per the pre-registered analysis plan, we excluded missing data at the individual item level.
Any observations missing data for all of the the predictor variables and the outcome variable (ability rating) were excluded from analyses.
Following these methods, 21 observations were excluded from the personality-only regression (n = 369) and 17 were excluded from the personality and behavior regression (n = 373).

text.text: We performed a principal components analysis on the personality variables to summarize the variance in the sample.
The principal components analysis reduced the 17 personality variables into a series of components that described a portion of the variance in the sample.

Based on the scree plot of the components and supported by evidence from Horn's parallel analysis, we selected the first four components which collectively describe 66.3% of the variance in the sample (Figure 2).

text.text: The four personality components can be described by the variables weighted the heaviest (magnitude > 0.3) within each component (Table 1).

text.text: For ease of interpretation, we have reversed the signs on all loadings for the components which contained primarily negative loadings.
Personality component 1 captures 24% of the total variance and we refer to this personality trait as confident.
The confident trait pairs high levels confidence, boldness, intelligence, initiative, and persistence with low levels of timidness and nervousness.
The internal consistency for the most heavily weighted variables is high (ω = 0.85) for the absolute values of the loadings.

Personality component 2 describes 22% of the variance and is characterized by positive representations of hyperactivity, excitability, and impulsiveness and negative representations of calmness and patience (active trait) (ω = 0.82).
Personality component 3 (11%) contained positive loadings of sociability and friendliness (social trait) with high internal consistency (ω = 0.92).
Lastly, personality component 4 (9%) contained positive weightings on trainability, obedience, nervousness, timidness, and hyperactivity (biddable trait), with low internal consistency (ω = 0.11).

Univariate regressions suggest that the confident personality trait (β = 0.32, SE = 0.02, t = 15.93) and biddable personality trait (β = 0.14, SE = 0.04, t = 3.27) were both associated with higher ratings on herding ability.
For non-personality fixed effects, we see that intact dogs (vs. spayed/neutered) were rated more highly in herding ability (β = -0.52, SE = 0.11, t = -4.75).
The yard environment was the only working environment not associated with overall herding ability.
We combined the predictors of interest in a linear mixed regression model to predict overall herding ability.

In the end, the best fit model with the highest Bayes factor when compared against the reference model included gonad removal status, utility work environment, trial work environment, and personality traits proactive and active (BF > 1000) (Table S4).

text.text: The best-fit model did not include any random effects.
The inclusion of the proactive and active traits indicates that both personality and behavioral variables are associated with overall herding ability.

From the included traits we see that overall herding ability was greater in dogs with higher levels of natural ability and confidence, and more skill at anticipation and many of the more concrete herding behaviors (e.g., cover, break, gather, etc.).

On the other hand, the inclusion of the active trait indicates some positive effects of more excitability, impulsiveness, and hyperactivity and potential negative effects of greater patience and calmness.
Compared to the proactive trait (β = 0.72), the standardized regression coefficient for the active trait (β = 0.04) is very small.
The active is contributing less to the model than the proactive trait.
Our third research question asked whether dog personality and owner-rated herding ability differ across breeds and countries.
We employed the same personality instrument (HDAF-P) and overall ability survey item as Wilson and colleagues (2022) designed and used for their study (see Methods for details).

text.text: For this analysis, we compared personality variables and overall herding ability ratings between Wilson et al.'s Australian kelpies (n = 228) and our American sample (n = 372, 64% border collies) (Table 3).

text.text: The American dogs showed strong evidence (Bayes factor > 3) for lower scores on confidence (USA = 3.85 ± 0.97, AUS = 4.14 ± 0.86, BF10 = 65.4), calmness (USA = 3.36 ± 1.09, AUS = 3.63 ± 1.07, BF10 = 5.9), patience (USA = 3.18 ± 1.08, AUS = 3.49 ± 0.99, BF10 = 34.4), hyperactivity (USA = 2.45 ± 1.14, AUS = 2.78 ± 1.24, BF10 = 19.5), and friendliness (USA = 4.11 ± 1.05, AUS = 4.33 ± 0.84, BF10 = 3.3).

text.text: There was not enough evidence to determine whether the average overall herding ability ratings differed between the samples (USA = 3.68 ± 0.86, AUS = 3.85 ± 0.84, BF10 = 1.3).
In addition to the pre-registered analyses, we performed a series of exploratory post hoc analyses.
Type of Herding Experience.
We investigated the relationship between herding environment and herding ability by directly comparing dogs with different herding experiences.
Dogs who had experience herding in both farm and trial settings (n = 231) received the highest ability ratings on average (M = 3.8).
Dogs with only farm experience (n = 102) had the next highest mean rating (M = 3.5), followed by dogs with only trial experience (n = 12, M = 3.4).
Mean ability rating differed between the dogs with only farm experience and with experience in both farm and trial settings (M = 0.4, 95% CI [0.2, 0.6], t(203.7) = 3.3, p = .001).
We did not statistically compare the trial-only group to the other groups due to the limited sample size (n = 12).
Amount of Herding Experience.
Next, we explored how the amount of herding experience a dog had related to ability rating.
For dogs with trial experience, the number of trials a dog participated in was correlated with ability rating (ρ = .20, p < .001).
text.formatted: For dogs with trial experience, the number of trials a dog participated in was correlated with ability rating (ρ = .20, p < .001).

text.text: A linear regression showed that number of trials competed in predicted herding ability (β = 0.01, SE = 0.00, t = 3.73, p < 0.001).
text.formatted: A linear regression showed that number of trials competed in predicted herding ability (β = 0.01, SE = 0.00, t = 3.73, p < 0.001).

text.text: However, this effect disappeared once we controlled for age (β = 0.02, SE = 0.01, t = 1.76, p = 0.080).
Age, Sex, and Gonad Status.
Age was not significantly correlated with overall ability (ρ = -.02, p = 1.000) or a significant predictor in a univariate linear regression (b = 0.00, 95% CI [-0.03, 0.03]).
The association between age and ability only existed when controlling for the other predictors in the best-fit multivariate regression.
Like age, sex of the dog was a predictor in the multivariate model but not a significant correlate (ρ = .06, p = 1.000) or predictor on its own (b = 0.15, 95% CI [-0.06, 0.36]).
However, gonad status was also included in the best-fit multivariate model and both correlated with (ρ = -.22, p = .024) and predicted overall ability on its own (b = -0.50, 95% CI [-0.71, -0.28]).
We have shown that herding behaviors contribute to herding performance in addition to personality.
But we did not directly assess whether adding behaviors to the models is better than having personality alone.
To test this, trimmed the data to only the participants who had data for both the personality and the behavioral variables (n = 365).
We then re-ran the two models and compared them using Bayes factors calculated from Bayes Information Criterion (BIC).
There was strong evidence (BF > 1000) that the personality and behavior model captured the observed data better than the personality-only model.
text.formatted: There was strong evidence (BF > 1000) that the personality and behavior model captured the observed data better than the personality-only model.

text.text: Note that the traits (PCA components) in the personality and behavior model are composed of more variables (n = 28) than the personality-only model (n = 17) because there are behaviors as well as personality variables.
However, both models have the same number of predictors, giving them equal model complexity for the Bayes Information Criterion.
The better fit of the personality and behavior model is likely due to the traits better capturing herding ability.
Breed Differences.
Lastly, we explored breed differences by comparing the border collies (n = 239) in our American sample to the kelpies in Wilson et al.'s (2022) Australian sample.
text.formatted: Lastly, we explored breed differences by comparing the border collies (n = 239) in our American sample to the kelpies in <ref type="bibr">Wilson et al.'s (2022)</ref> Australian sample.

text.text: Like the American sample as a whole, the border collies were less confident (border collie = 3.80 ± 1.00, kelpie = 4.14 ± 0.86, BF10 = 132.3) and less patient (border collie = 3.23 ± 1.06, kelpie = 3.49 ± 0.99, BF10 = 4.0) than the kelpies.

However, the border collies were also more timid (border collie = 2.31 ± 1.07, kelpie = 2.01 ± 0.93, BF10 = 11.8) and impulsive (border collie = 2.87 ± 1.13, kelpie = 2.58 ± 1.13, BF10 = 4.0) than the kelpies.
In this study, we replicated and built upon previous literature addressing the complex associations between dogs personality, behavior, and herding ability.
The first research question investigated which personality variables in dogs are associated with owner-reported overall herding ability by replicating Wilson et a. (2022).

text.text: The personality traits in our sample are similar to those reported by Wilson et al. (2022), but their best-fit regression model included four PCA components while our model only included two.

text.text: Our best-fit model for predicting herding ability rating included both the confident and biddable personality traits.
The confident trait describes a dog that is intelligent and does their job without hesitation.
Dogs with the biddable personality trait are high on variables related to ease of training, energy level, and fear.
The variables most heavily weighted in the confident and biddable traits are also included in Wilson et al.'s personality components.
The confident trait is in line with prior literature (e.g., Svartberg (2002)) supporting a positive association between confidence/boldness, intelligence, trainability, and working performance.
text.formatted: The confident trait is in line with prior literature (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Svartberg (2002)</ref>) supporting a positive association between confidence/boldness, intelligence, trainability, and working performance.

text.text: While confident is low on fear, biddable is high.

Fear is often found to be undesirable in working dogs (Dollion et al., 2019; Rooney et al., 2016; Scott & Fuller, 2020; Svartberg, 2002), but our evidence suggests the story might not be so simple in herding dogs.

text.text: Expanding on the replication, our second research question asked whether a combination of personality and behavioral variables could predict herding ability.
We found that a combination of both personality and behavioral variables significantly predict overall herding ability.
This model was more complex than the best-fit personality model and accordingly explained more variance.
Both the proactive and active traits appeared in the personality and behavior model.
The herding behaviors in the proactive trait collectively paint a picture of a dog that is skilled at reading and anticipating the actions of livestock.
The active trait, on the other hand, describes a hyperactive dog that is impulsive and excitable.
Both traits predicted higher herding ability ratings, though the proactive trait offers more predictive power within the model.
The weighting of individual behavioral variables within the traits suggests that some herding behaviors are more relevant than others.
This supports owner's perceptions that some herding behaviors are more important to overall herding ability than others (Early et al., 2019).
text.formatted: This supports owner's perceptions that some herding behaviors are more important to overall herding ability than others <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Early et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: While the personality and behavior model is more likely to produce the observed data, we do not put too much weight in this comparison.

The personality and behavior model is more complex than the personality-only model and would be expected to perform better in a test that does not account for the complexity captured by the PCA components.
Future studies could address this limitation by designing analysis plans with the goal of comparing models.
Working environment played a role in the best-fit model for predicting herding ability.
Dogs that work in utility settings (a combination of large and small spaces) and compete in herding trials were also more likely to be rated highly.
Exploratory analyses expanded this finding to show that dogs with experience working in both farm and trial settings had significantly higher ability ratings than those with only farm experience.
Our sample did not have a large enough group of dogs with trial-only experience to statistically compare with the other two groups.
However, the mean ability rating of dogs that only had trial experience was the lowest of the three groups.
Of the dogs with trial experience, those who competed in more trials were given higher ability ratings than those who competed in fewer trials.
In a univariate linear regression, number of trials a dog competed in predicted herding ability.
When taking age into account, however, the effect of number of trials was no longer significant.

Future studies could systematically examine the effect of herding environment on herding ability by collecting longitudinal data to account for age and purposefully sampling across working environments.
Age was present in both of our best-fit multivariate regression models, with younger dogs receiving higher overall ability ratings than older dogs.
However, the association between age and ability is not simple enough to be captured in a correlation or univariate regression.
The relationship between age and ability only emerges once we have controlled for the effects of a number of other predictors.
Similarly, sex of the dog was a predictor in the multivariate model but not a significant correlate or predictor on its own.
After controlling for age, gonad status, work environment, personality, and behavior, male dogs received higher ability ratings than female dogs.
Gonad status was also included in the best-fit multivariate model and both correlated with and predicted overall ability on its own.
Owners rated intact dogs significantly higher on their herding ability than spayed/neutered dogs.
Neutering dogs, particularly males, impacts their behavior (Arroube & Pereira, 2025; Fadel et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Neutering dogs, particularly males, impacts their behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Arroube & Pereira, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Fadel et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Our findings could suggest that the post-neuter behavioral presentation is less useful for herding than the intact presentation.
On the other hand, owners may be more likely to keep their most skilled herding dogs intact for breeding purposes.
The effect of gonad removal on ability rating could be specifically studied -and potentially ruled out as an explanation -with a pre-post research design.
In our last research question we compared our American study sample to the kelpies in Wilson et al.'s Australian study sample.
We found that the American dogs were rated as less confident, calm, patient, hyperactive, and friendly than the Australian dogs.
Differences between these samples suggest that personality could differ between the American and Australian populations of herding dogs.
As Wilson and colleagues (2022) point out, geographic regions can create different environmental pressures that favor dogs with particular behavioral traits.
Beyond geography, humans play a large role in the selection and breeding of dogs.
Americans and Australians could prefer dogs with different personality profiles.
Breed is another possible driver of differences between the samples.
We explored the effect of breed in this comparison by repeating the analyses with a subset of our sample that included only border collies.
Compared to the Australian kelpies, our border collies were rated as less confident and patient, and more timid and impulsive.
The personalities of the border collies may be driving the observed differences between our samples as a whole.
Border collies and kelpies are used for the same general purpose, but they are two distinct breeds with unique herding styles.
The present study cannot untangle the influence of breed from that of country.
More research specifically designed to examine the differences between populations of herding dogs would allow for greater generalization of findings.
Our findings are limited by the cross-sectional design of this study.
Though our sample represented a wide geographical range within the United States, we cannot generalize to herding dogs living in other countries.
Similarly, our sample predominantly consists of border collies, limiting our ability to generalize across herding breeds.
As we note, the present study cannot separate the effects of breed and location on dog personality.
Our personality and behavioral variables represent different types of ratings.
The personality ratings capture the owner's perception of how strongly the dog presents the personality adjective (e.g. boldness).
On the other hand, the behavioral ratings record the owner's perception of how skilled the dog is at the behavior listed.
While this distinction may seem slight, it means that values on these two variables must be interpreted differently.
Behavioral variables in this study cannot tell us the intensity or "how much" of a behavior is desirable.
Skill level on behavioral variables and overall herding ability may be overlapping concepts.
This could explain the relatively high correlations between most of the behavior variables and the herding ability rating.
The present study focuses on dog owner perceptions of dog traits and abilities.
There is evidence to support the validity of owner report for dog personality and behavioral variables.
However, we do not claim that owner perceptions are accurate representations of some underlying "true" level of herding ability.
The construct that we are operationalizing with owner ratings of herding ability is a human perception of herding.
Importantly, these perceptions are what drive decision making about herding dog populations.

Though we did not measure ability directly, measuring perceptions is useful since these perceptions inform decisions about which dogs are selected and bred for herding, as well as how they are trained.
Ultimately, our goal is to improve the success rates of herding dogs.
This study can inform decision making and training for the success of adult herding dogs in the United States.
Prior literature suggests that dog personality and behavior are influenced by a combination of genetics and environment (Fratkin et al., 2013; Salonen et al., 2023; Strandberg et al., 2025).

text.text: We provide evidence that these (potentially) heritable herding behaviors are linked to owner ratings of overall herding ability.
In line with previous literature, we suggest that selective breeding based on specific herding behaviors is a viable method for increasing overall herding ability over generations.
Beyond breeding, interventions can focus on variables that are susceptible to environmental influence.

text.text: Dogs that receive more training also tend to be rated as more trainable (Kubinyi et al., 2009).
text.formatted: Dogs that receive more training also tend to be rated as more trainable <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Kubinyi et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: While this relationship is not necessarily causal or unidirectional, Kubinyi and colleagues found that the dogs that were rated the lowest on trainability in their sample were dogs over the age of three who had received no professional training.
This provides initial evidence that training itself may increase the personality variable of trainability in dogs.
Training for herding dogs already focuses on herding behaviors, but could more intentionally target the behaviors identified in this study to make the most of training efforts.
Additionally, training dogs to work in different environments could be beneficial.
Dogs who frequently participate in herding trials may practice or learn new skills that benefit their overall herding ability.
Taken together, this evidence suggests that training may be able to increase levels of personality and behavioral variables that are associated with herding ability in dogs.
Herding dogs play a critical role in the management of livestock worldwide.
Yet we know little about the factors underlying their herding performance.
In this study, we have replicated previous work in a new sample of herding dogs and expanded the narrow body of knowledge on herding dogs.
The personality and behavioral traits identified in this study may be used to inform dog owner's decisions about dog career paths and training efforts for herding dog success.
